utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very good afternoon to everybody. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And another additional thank you for preparing us with an additional proffer so that we know what we can expect today. You have seen the time limits of today, and let's try that we can conclude this witness by today. And therefore, without -- explicitly without imposing a time limit now, I would ask the Defence if possible to conclude somewhere after 2 and a half hours, up to 3 hours, and then later on, the Prosecution also limiting itself to the absolute necessary that we then can conclude finally on or about 7.00. I can't see any objections. May I therefore ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you. Once again, to be on the safe side, no protective measures requested by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Thank you for coming --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- to The Hague. And welcome. Can you hear me in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to give your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. You're a Defence witness. Mr. Lukic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Krejic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and together with John Ostojic, I represent the defence of Dr. Stakic before this Tribunal. Firstly, I would kindly ask you to give us some of your personal data, starting with first things first. Can you please for the record give us your full name, the first name and the last name.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: My name is Radovan Krejic. My father's name was Milos. I was born on the 13th of November, 1946. I live in Prijedor. I've lived there since 1990. Before that, I lived in Sanski Most, which is 30 kilometres away from Prijedor. Is there anything else you would like me to tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please also tell us your profession.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the law school in Belgrade, and I currently work in the company which deals with the production of energy in the city plant in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever work in the self-interest community of health protection?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Until four years ago, I worked in that institution, which used to be called the self-interest community of health insurance. Now it's the healthcare fund. So all of my life before that, I've spent working in the institutions providing health-care and looking after health-care.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, have you ever been a member of any political party and what party was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, I was a member of the then communist league of Yugoslavia for a period of time. Immediately before the war, I was a member of the so-called reformist forces of Yugoslavia, which were led by Anto Markovic. That was immediately prior to the beginning of the war. And as of recently, I have been a member of the social democrats, that is, the independent social democrats led by Mr. Milorad Dodik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of the Serbian democratic party?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, I have never been one of their members. I cooperated with them when they were in power, and I still cooperate with the organs of that party to the extent to which my job is related and connected with the organs of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: For a brief period of time, I was a deputy. I was not elected. I was appointed. But it lasted for a short period of time. I believe it was in late 1993, towards the end of 1993 in any case.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: It was the end of 1992 and beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you the president of the commission for social affairs, which was established by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the SDS, that is, the then president of the SDS, Mr. Simo Miskovic, invited me and suggested that I should run the commission which was in charge of proposing the best organisation of the activities in which I was engaged. So this was part of the overall social services, and I was in charge of health care.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As the president of that commission, did you participate at meetings, at SDS meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: On two occasions, I was present at the sessions of the municipal board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After your personal data, I would like to ask you something about the year 1992. Firstly, as the director of the self-interest community for health care in charge of the Prijedor region, which municipalities did your office cover?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: We covered four municipalities that belonged to the region of Prijedor at the time. Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanska Dubica, and Bosanski Novi, with some 230.000 inhabitants all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you in 1992, in connection with your work, ever talk to Mr. Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the topic of that conversation? Can you describe how this conversation went on.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I had several meetings with Mr. Cehajic. He was the president of the Municipal Assembly, and we knew each other well because he used to be my teacher before that in the grammar school. And we also are natives of the same town, of Sanski Most. And if you are referring to the conversation that I had with him regarding the problem of the financing of health care, then the conversation went like this, if I can give you some more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Immediately prior to the beginning of the war, due to the complicated situation that we faced at the time, Muhamed Cehajic as the president of the assembly called me and asked me to -- actually demanded from me to channel the money from the contributions for health care, and that we then channelled to the health-care institutions that shouldn't be channelled in the ratios that were prior to that established in the former self-interest community. That this money should be kept in Prijedor rather to be sent for the financing of health institutions in Bosanska Dubica, Sanski Most, and Bosanski Novi because the SDS was there in power. I believe there was already a confrontation in place between the SDS and the SDA, and I believe that in the municipalities that I have just mentioned, the complete leadership of those municipalities was from the SDS. So he believed that all the funds had to be kept in Prijedor, so that they wouldn't be used for the purposes for which they were not intended. I told him that he was not informed enough about the way we allocated the funds, and I told him that all the funds that we collect from all the employees in the four municipalities are paid into the Giro account of the republican fund in Sarajevo, and then from the republican fund in Sarajevo, according to the allotment, they are then returned to Prijedor to a collective Giro account that I was disposing with. And then I was the one who allocated the funds into all the four municipalities into the so-called basic organisations or the branches which are managed by the buses which are subordinate to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are just going to interrupt for a moment, because my learned friend, the Prosecutor, wishes to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness please be asked to slow down because it's very, very hard to follow at this pace, and I don't think the interpreters would last for another half an hour if we do continue at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is indeed ambiguous. We tried to finalise that as soon as possible but I was aware there were real problems to follow your speech, and I am grateful that you do it this way, but please, slow down a little bit. Thank you for your understanding, and thank you for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So let's try and slow down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: So I told Mr. Cehajic as the president of the municipal assembly of Prijedor -- I explained to him how we worked. And since their relations had not changed, we still worked according to the same regulations. I told him that I would continue working in keeping with the regulations that were still in effect. In other words, that I would continue distributing the funds that I receive in the Giro account according to the way that was prescribed for my fund. Mr. Cehajic reacted rather harshly. He threatened me. He used a threatening tone when he asked me to obey him and to keep the money in my Giro account until further notice. I persisted in my views. I did not accept his suggestions. And finally, Mr. Cehajic threatened me that he would remove me from my office of director should I continue to work in that way. I had to draw Mr. Cehajic's attention again to his authority, and I told him that my position and the work that I did was not under the authority of the municipal organs, but that I was rather appointed by my own body which was called the assembly of the self-interest community of Prijedor, which also prescribed regulations for the region of Prijedor in the area of health care, and they were the ones who appointed me as director, and I reported to them for the job that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cehajic, what was his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, he was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About that time or immediately after that, were you approached by Mr. Mirza Mujadzic, who was the president of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mujadzic was the president of the SDA, and his office happened to be in the same building where I worked. He was on the ground floor and I was on the first floor, one floor above. So we would come across each other very often. We would often see each other, occasionally, or from time to time. He would even pop into my office to have a chat and to exchange views on the situation that we faced and on the possibilities to organise health care because he was a physician, and he was very much interested in what we did. When Mr. Cehajic and I fell out, Dr. Mujadzic came to visit me after that. He must have been informed by Mr. Cehajic what had happened. And he tried to mediate, and he tried to achieve some sort of an understanding. He said that there was no need for any tensions. He said that Mr. Cehajic was not right in asking me to do what he asked me to do. On the second day, one day after that, probably upon the insistence of Mr. Mujadzic, Mr. Cehajic came to my office, and once again we had a conversation about the overall issue, about that problem. And this time, I asked my closest associate, Mr. Sead Cikota to join us in the conversation. He was my deputy in my position of the director of the Prijedor fund. Since he was -- is a Muslim, that is. In the light of the overall situation that prevailed at the time, I believe it was best for him to join us in the conversation in order to help my positions be understood as best as possible. I wanted to continue working as I did before that. And that's what I wanted him to help me with. After that conversation, Mr. Cehajic, so to say, admitted that my views were right, but still harboured ill feelings towards me. And that persisted throughout the future period. The conversation showed that I was absolutely right in terms of the implementation of the regulations that were then in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. -- Is Mr. Sead Cikota still alive?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is still alive. Mr. Cikota was in some sort of a prison during the crisis period in the summer of 1992, and later on he was released. It was proven that he was innocent. And for a brief period of time, he was in Trnopolje in the reception centre; and later on, at his own request, he left and went to(redacted). And he still resides there with his family. He comes from (redacted) very often. We are now very good friends. He is now retired. We helped him to get his pension. He receives his pensions -- pension regularly. He visited me last new year, and if you need, you can check that with -- all this with Mr. Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that he was incarcerated for a brief period of time, are you referring to the investigation centre in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the investigation centre in Omarska, was he transferred to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you visit him there in Trnopolje, and what you see there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I visited him once after I had been informed that he was in Trnopolje. Trnopolje was very close to Prijedor. And I was told that I could easily go there, that -- and since those were all refugees together with an associate of ours, who was formerly the director of the hospital, Mr. Rodic, Juto Rodic, I went to Trnopolje, and I saw Mr. Cikota. I spent some time with him. I thought maybe I could give him a ride home. But he insisted on staying there because he had still not arranged his departure papers. He wanted to go abroad, and his papers were still not ready for that. He had still not done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about the year 1992. Before the war broke out, before the takeover of Prijedor, did Muslims, Croats, and Serbs leave Prijedor? Can you tell us if you are aware of that? When did you become aware of that? When did you first notice that, and who was leaving?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: It was the population that was leaving Prijedor. I wouldn't say Muslims, Croats, Serbs. Everybody was leaving towards the end of 1991, throughout 1991 when the war broke out in Croatia and when the tensions increased in the former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the situation became complicated in the politics, people were scared. They were afraid that the conflicts would break out in Prijedor, and they started leaving. They were headed for different areas of Yugoslavia, and even abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again, Your Honour, but out of an abundance of caution, would we be able to have the country that appears on page 9, lines 11 and 12 redacted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. If we want to be extremely cautious, it seems to be better. May I ask Madam Registrar to redact the country of residence of the third person mentioned from the transcript, please. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you and when send from Prijedor any members of your family?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think it was in April my daughter left, together with my daughter-in-law. My sister-in-law, my brother's wife, she was about to give birth, and she had to be put away somewhere safe so that she could give birth peacefully. So I took the opportunity, so to speak, and I helped my daughter and my sister-in-law to go to Novi Sad so they could be in a safe place. My daughter, for her education, and my sister-in-law for her birth. And then later on, I also sent my son away to Vojvodina for his education so that he could attend school regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from people leaving Prijedor, those who were in Prijedor who were leaving, was anyone arriving in Prijedor at that same time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Those who were leaving Prijedor were mostly students, children, women, unemployed women; those who were in a position to leave Prijedor without any consequences for their jobs. Later on, some even quit their jobs and left as things got worse. People were arriving in Prijedor, mostly people from Croatia, because the war had already begun in Croatia, and all those who could, all those who had family in Prijedor or business connections, those who had someone to go to, they came. So both Prijedor and Sanski Most received a lot of people because there were many people from our region who worked in Croatia or in Slovenia very often. First, their families came, and then after that men followed suit. They would come to Prijedor and also to the other towns in the Bosanska Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was by and large the ethnicity of people who were arriving in Prijedor? And did this already begin in 1991, and did it continue in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Mostly this began in 1999 [sic], but then the scale of the whole thing kept increasing. In the early days, people of all ethnic backgrounds were arriving. It was more important where someone was actually from physically, where they lived, than their ethnicity. Most often the people arriving were Serbs because there were very many Serbs working in the other republics. But then Muslims and Croats kept coming, too, those who had family in Prijedor, Sanski Most, or any of the other towns. It was quite simple. People were trying to get away from a war-torn area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The arrival of these refugees, did it cause problems in terms of financing health care, health insurance, in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Whenever you have a huge influx of population, expenditure tends to rise. It costs money to receive these people. Prior to that, obviously there were requests for health insurance in our health institution, in our health institutions, and those were on the rise. It was necessary to get extra funds to get enough money to give these people proper treatment. Mostly, we were talking about children who had a right to free medical assistance regardless of whether they had health insurance or not because those were the regulations in place then as now. Children up to 15 years of age, and elderly people above 60 years of age had a right to free medical care regardless of whether they were paying contributions or not. And from that point of view, we had an obligation to secure the finances needed to give those people medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you at that time address the republican health fund in Sarajevo to help you with that situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We looked at our finances, and knew exactly how much money we needed to secure the bare minimum of what was needed in terms of providing these people who kept coming in with medical assistance. I first addressed my own director, and the organs of the republican fund, the bodies of the republican fund for help. Because as part of the republican fund, we had solidarity funds, the so-called solidarity funds, which means that part of the republican funds would be set aside, that was 10 per cent at that time, for the solidarity funds to help the areas which were undeveloped, so to speak, or to send assistance in emergency cases. As those funds, those 10 per cent were insufficient, I also spoke to municipal assemblies, or the relevant bodies in the municipal assemblies that had to do with health care. I spoke to the municipal bodies in Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanska Dubica, and Bosanski Novi. I requested additional funds so that we would be able to cover the extra expenses incurred by the need to provide these new people with medical treatment, all the people who were coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you eventually solve this problem, the problem that came about when a great number of refugees came to the different municipalities in Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: We did receive additional funds from the republican solidarity funds, and the relevant organs of the municipalities that I referred to, the four municipalities, granted us the possibility of introducing additional rates of contribution for all those who were employed in our region in order to get enough money, get enough funds, to provide the people who had arrived with proper medical assistance. We agreed on this throughout the different finance departments of these four municipalities. And then our own bodies adopted a decision where the exact amounts of this additional contribution were defined from which the -- our extra expenses would then be financed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the increased need due to the influx of refugees, did you at that time also have problems with supplies? Because the previous supply lines had been cut because of the war in Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Usually, before that situation came about, we used the supply lines which originated most often in Zagreb and Ljubljana. Very often from Belgrade and Novi Sad, too. We used some of the capacities in Sarajevo, too. But there were obviously transportation problems and problems arose in our communication with our former partners. So as I was the one who alongside with the other directors of health institutions, I'm talking about pharmacies and hospitals, was in charge of financing the whole thing, we agreed to set up communication with companies based in Serbia, because they were still in a position to provide us with the necessary medicines and medical equipment. Even from Slovenia and from the Pliva company in Zagreb, we could still obtain certain things that we needed. But only through companies based in Serbia, for the simple reason that there was no communication at that time between Croatia, Slovenia, and Bosnia. So we used companies based in Belgrade to get certain medicines that were only produced by the Pliva company in Zagreb, and that were sold across Europe. That's why even during the war we were able to obtain these products in Prijedor for the newborn children. Those were mostly anti-tuberculosis medicines and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already said, but can you please elaborate now, the hierarchy of your own self-interest organisation or the fund and the relation between this -- with the Municipal Assembly and its executive organ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: We were organised at the Republican level, the Republican level of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was such a thing as the republican fund or the republican SIZ as we used to refer to it, for health insurance. Within the framework of the republican SIZ, the fund, we had regional organisations. Those were branch offices of health insurance across the Prijedor region, the Banja Luka region, the Tuzla region, the Mostar region, and so on and so forth. I think there was eight such regions all together. What was the hierarchy? It was from the top, that's the republican level, through the branch offices throughout the regions, down to the low-level basic offices as we referred to them at that time in municipalities. So every municipality had a branch office for health insurance where health cards were issued, and people would go there for their basic rights that they were -- things they were entitled to under the health insurance policies. We collected the funds for health insurance, and we were in charge of distributing the funds down to the branch offices. We did not have a direct relationship with the municipal organs, I would say, because we were working in a field which was vertically linked from Sanski Most all the way to up Sarajevo. That's how we used to define it. Our only obligation to the municipal bodies was to report once a year and give them the information that they demanded from us. Those were data on the general health situation among the population, because they had an official in the municipality who was in charge of the health insurance. And our fund would then forward the information demanded by their officer, and then together we would draw up an annual report on the health situation among the population in the area that we covered. It was the usual sort of information, birth rate, death rate, the amount of medicines that was used up throughout the year in the municipality. All the information that was relevant for health insurance. And then this report would be forwarded to the municipal bodies, and I'm talking about the Executive Board. And through the Executive Board, the report would reach the Municipal Assembly. Once a year, they would review these reports, and they would send us their feedback or their proposals, if they had any in reaction to our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At the level of the former Yugoslavia, was there an association of communities, and what was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's one thing I forgot to say. We weren't directly linked to each other within that association, but our republican fund was part of the association of health care communities across the former Yugoslavia. There were six such funds within the association, and the job of this association of communities was to coordinate the work of all the republican funds, the SIZ organisations, the self-interest organisations, and to adopt the norms and the regulations that would be valid and binding for all the republican SIZ organisations. Those were the basic regulations mostly governing the issues concerning medical treatment provided to citizens from one -- from a different republic, medical treatment given them in the territory of a different republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly or its Executive Board, in addition to having the power to demand information for you -- from you, did they in any way have the power to govern your work or to give you -- or to give orders to any of the organisational units within your fund?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No. In practical terms, we were not directly in touch with the municipal bodies. As I said, the contact we had was based on these reports. We would send them reports on our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following the takeover, you addressed Mr. -- Dr. Milomir Stakic. Will you please tell us why you addressed him and what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: In the period when the takeover took place in Prijedor, I was gone from Prijedor for a while, for a week. I spent a week in Yugoslavia. And when I was back, I heard about what had happened. I called Dr. Stakic because I knew him personally. He was a doctor who worked in our -- who was a part of our health system. And I asked him in connection with what I heard had happened, whether there were any new instructions concerning our own work. And he said that there would be no changes, and that we should just continue working as before and that our fund would keep on operating just like before. He said the only thing I should do is stick to the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your health insurance fund after the takeover, how did it treat its own holders of health insurance? Did you treat people differently depending on their nationality, on their ethnicity, or did you give the same kind of service to everyone, or did it depend on anything else?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: As there had been no changes in the regulations until the next summer, because that's when certain regulations, certain changes to the regulations were in place, we just continued work as before. There were no changes in the practical sense. It's only that in some areas, the need -- the demand for health insurance increased, and in some it decreased. I mean the war later on and people being wounded. But we worked the same way as before. We just checked the patients' IDs, we would send them somewhere to be treated. We would refer them to doctors. So we never distinguished between people. I would sign, for example, references for someone to be sent for treatment outside Bosnia and Herzegovina, to Novi Sad or to Belgrade. And believe me, never, not on a single occasion did I check who was the person being sent. It was an automatic process. We had a committee on which doctors sat from the different areas of medicine, and they would usually write up an opinion that a certain patient was to be sent to a particular kind of medical institution. I would just sign this reference, this decision, and most often I didn't even look at the name of the person being referred. I just wanted to see whether qualified people, doctors, did indeed believe that this person was to be sent to a particular institution. And it was an automatic thing for me. I would just sign these papers. However, if I may just add something that I've just remembered, later when mobilisation callups started arriving, and the number of people leaving for -- to join the army increased, the secretariat for National Defence in Prijedor requested that I inform them about being -- that the people who had joined the army would be sent for medical treatment outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I suppose they were afraid that there would be subjective decisions concerning where soldiers were being sent for treatment. And they insisted to have an insight into the basis for our decisions to send people for treatment to Belgrade, that sort of thing. And during a certain period, we did inform the secretariat for National Defence who we were sending and where. We would provide them with lists of patients being sent away for treatment. And this went on for about a month. And then after a month or two, this ceased altogether, because they were satisfied, the people from the secretariat, that we were basing our references on objective factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you also provide the funds for the treatment of people in the most serious cases, even for those who did not pay the contributions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I already said that it was our legal obligation to provide the funds for the treatment of children and elderly people. In the war, it was very rarely that we checked whether contributions had actually been paid. The situation was very difficult. The financial situation was very difficult. And in dire straits, obviously the level of solidarity among people tends to increase. So when we were dealing with serious illnesses and serious cases, we would grant the treatment even for the most serious cases without checking whether the contributions had been paid. We would send them to the largest clinical hospitals, but in such cases we would also send the request to the ministry of finances to get a refund on those expenses. According to the then-prevailing regulations, the state had to provide for the health care of those people who are not insured, who are not beneficiaries of health insurance, but for procedural reasons, in order to speed up the treatment of these people, we would send them to the clinics first, and then when the clinics would in turn send us their bills, we would then send our request for refunds to the state fund.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the situations in which you sent people outside of the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you told us how this was funded and you explained to us what the procedure looked like for anybody who wished to be treated outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did these persons have to have some special permits or authorisations in order to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina and to travel outside Bosnia and Herzegovina? And who was it who issued such permits?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: When the conflicts escalated, all the citizens fit for military service, whenever they travelled, for whatsoever reason, they had to obtain a permit from the competent military bodies. Those permits were issued by the secretariat for the National Defence. And those permits were used to cross the border towards Yugoslavia. And when we travelled throughout the region, since there were the so-called checkpoints between different towns, we would be issued by some sort of a laissez-passer or permits from our police, from the secretariat for the interior. I had such a permit, such a laissez-passer, which was a permanent pass, because I would go very often to Sanski Most, Bosanska Dubica, or Bosanski Novi to perform my official duties. And I was issued that pass by the chief of the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify something with regard to the medical board, the board of experts who were in charge of approving people's departure for treatment outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. Was that a novelty or was it something that existed even before the war and that exists even today?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: These were medical boards who are put in place in order to avoid the misuse and -- of health funds, because the expenses of treatment in the biggest clinical hospitals tend to be very high, that's why these medical boards are in charge of inspecting the medical documents prepared by the patient's doctor, based on their insight and based on their experience and expertise, they will justify the need for the person to be sent outside the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for any kind of treatment. Within the borders of the republic, we were able to refer a patient to any health institution. However, whenever the treatment was requested to be performed in a large clinic, a board should be set up to review these documents. These boards existed before the war and they still exist today for such purposes. The board -- such a board usually consists of specialists working in the Prijedor hospital and health centres or medical centres which are covered by the Prijedor SIZ, the self-interest community. A permanent member of the commission was a doctor who was my assistant and who was an affiliate with the self-interest health insurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please put in perspective the relationship between your fund and the military fund of health insurance. Can you tell us whether these are two separate, different, institutions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: They are completely separate. We did not have anything whatsoever to do with the treatment of the beneficiaries who were in the army. They had their separate insurance, and their treatment was funded from the funds at the level of the republican budget. This is the budget that was allocated for the ministry of Defence, and from those funds, some funds were allocated for the treatment of members of the army. We did not have any contacts with the military health-care institution, with the military insurance. Our only contact with them was in cases when we referred our patients, that is, civilians, to military health-care institutions, military hospitals. And that happened before the war; that still happens today in cases when a patient requires the highest level of treatment. And in those cases, patients would be referred to the military medical academy in Belgrade, which is the largest and the most state-of-the-art institution in the former Yugoslavia, and we still do the same today. But that is the contact with the hospital which is a military hospital, but also admits a number of civilians. And this is where our job stops. The military medical academy provides the treatment and sends us the bills, bills our fund for covering the expenses of such a treatment. And this is the only contact we had with military institutions. I would go from time to time to the military hospital in Belgrade to regulate our financial relationships with that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If any of your beneficiaries were to be injured, would you also cover the expenses of their treatment, or would it be the military health-insurance fund who would be paying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: As a rule, it should be the military insurance fund who provides for all the injured persons from the moment they issued the mobilisation callups to the moment when they returned home. But we did have sporadic situations due to the lack of material, equipment, both in our civilian fund and in the army fund. We would from time to time encounter some problems with regard to -- as to who was under the obligation to pay for the treatment of the injured persons. We encountered a situation which lasted for a long period of time during the war. The martial law was not in place, and military authorities would say that the able-bodied men were only called up for military drills, and they thought that it would be the civilian insurance -- health-insurance fund who had to pay for the treatment of their -- of the injured people. So we did that. And later on, this situation was resolved amongst the funds at the republican level. We did not have enough money to provide for the treatment of all the civilian beneficiaries, let alone those who were injured when they were doing their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the period between April and September of 1992, did you ever talk to the chief of the public security station in Prijedor, Mr. Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What can you recall from those contacts?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I knew Drljaca, the chief of the public security station, from before. We did not have many official contacts because we did not have anything in common in our two jobs. But I visited Mr. Drljaca at the beginning of the war because I knew him personally, and I tried to see if he could help me when he -- when the gentleman that I had mentioned, Mr. Sead Cikota was in Trnopolje, he was my close associate. And I thought that I should help him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The camp was Omarska.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: So I visited Mr. Drljaca in his office, and I asked him to help Sead to be released from the investigation centre. I talked to him for a long time. I wasn't well-informed for the reasons that Mr. Cikota had been taken to the investigation centre. And since I had known him for a long period of time, I did not see any valid reason for him to be interrogated, and I said to the chief of the public security station, and I asked him to speed up the procedure of Mr. Cikota's interrogation because I didn't see any elements for this man to be subject to any investigation. He then told me that if what I was saying was correct, that there shouldn't be any problems, that he is there together with a group of people who are fit for military service, militarily-aged men, and that after the investigation that had to be carried out according to their regulations, and if there were no elements for criminal prosecution, that he would be released. He convinced me, and he promised me, that he would speed up the procedure. I insisted on the procedure to be sped up because I thought there were no elements for the investigation in the first place. And that's how we left it off. He promised me that the procedure would be sped up, and that everything would be over soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it who told you that Mr. Sead Cikota was incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: From his wife. She called me on the telephone and told me that her husband had been taken away to Omarska. She didn't actually know where he was taken, but she had been informed that he would be taken to Omarska. And she asked for my assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you approach Mr. Drljaca and ask for his assistance and possible release of your friend and colleague?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Because he was the chief of the public security station, and I also told you that I had known him personally. So I believed that he was in the position to help me to resolve that problem, the problem of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in October 1992, the party in power in Prijedor at that time, the SDS, started an initiative for the removal of Dr. Milomir Stakic as the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I was not really involved in politics at that time, not much. But I was -- I was in town, and you know rumours did go around. People knew a lot of things even if you weren't involved in politics. And I knew that inside the SDS, there were certain clashes - that was the word around the town - clashes between leaders, both in the SDS and in the municipal military and police bodies. Word was that Dr. Stakic and Srdjo Srdic, who for a period of time was the president of the SDS and a deputy, were not really getting along in terms of their opinions. I knew both of them, because they both come from the medical field. And they said that Dr. Stakic and Srdjo Srdic were not really getting along well, and that their opinions were differing. But word was that their clash was quite serious, and that there were serious problems between them. And also that there were problems between the president of the SDS, the former president of the SDS, Srdjo Srdic, and Simo. That's also another thing that was being talked about. And I think for the same reasons, and at the request of a certain number of people from the municipal board of the SDS, there was a request for Dr. Stakic to be removed. On one later occasion, I attended a meeting of the municipal board of the SDS. I was a member of the committee for health -- for organising the health situation. And I was giving a report on the work of that commission. And at that meeting, requests were repeated for the removal of Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, may I ask now to go into private session for a few moments. We have to mention some names, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed Dr. Stakic. Can you tell us when you met him and how well you know him?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I've known Dr. Stakic since the days he started working as a doctor. I've spent practically the whole of my working life with the exception of the last several years working as part of the health system. I was assistant to the head of the health centre in Sanski Most. I was assistant to the head of the regional medical centre in Prijedor. And then I was the director of the SIZ fund. I knew doctors who were active. Dr. Stakic was very young when before the war he started working as a doctor in Omarska. I didn't know him very well at that time, but I got to know him better later as the vice-president of the municipality, then later as the president of the Municipal Assembly. And especially when he became the head of the health centre, we were then very close associates. We worked closely together. It was the nature of my job. I collaborated very closely with the heads of the health centres and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please, in a few words, describe Dr. Stakic's personality.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I believe Dr. Stakic is a young, ambitious doctor. He was considered a very successful doctor, too. My impression throughout the period when we worked together was I hope he won't get angry now, but he struck me as a person without enough experience in politics. I was his senior, and sometimes we would talk, and I would warn him a number of times about his lack of experience in politics. I told him that I didn't think it was a good time for him to be involved in politics, given the general circumstances and the times, given the responsibility that I thought was too much for him to handle in view of his experience. I openly advised him to go back to working as a doctor, especially in that period when he was under attack while he was the president of the assembly. I advised him to grab the opportunity and withdraw from politics and go back to working as a doctor, because that was where he could really make an important contribution. I knew he had been a brilliant student. I believed that he would be much more useful to the community working as a doctor than working as a politician. I think he is a very humanitarian person and a qualified physician. I really think it's such a shame that he didn't spend the whole of this period working as a doctor instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I have a question about you. You said that you had been co-opted as a deputy to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Were you removed from that position, and what was the reason for your removal? Tell us, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: As I told you, I was never a member of the SDS. But I was closely acquainted with Simo Miskovic, the president of the SDS. And we spent part of our childhood together. We grew up in the same building in Sanski Most. My father worked for the local court there, and his father worked for the police. So they also knew each other. But then at one point, they moved from Sanski Most, and then we met up again in Prijedor. I considered him a friend. When he became the president of the SDS, he insisted that I join the SDS. I was not inclined to join the party, to become a member of that party. You know what the times were like. There was a war. And I had my own take on that. I thought that there was -- in such a situation, there was nothing much to be done about it because the interests in a time of war were different and that party conflicts only had a negative effect on the entire -- on the overall situation in our area. We talked, and I told him that I was perfectly prepared to help as a professional and that I would use my qualifications and my knowledge to give my contribution to improve the circumstances in our area and the living conditions. It was on the basis of that that Simo first proposed me -- propose to appoint me as a member of the social affairs. He knew that I was familiar with my own area of work because I was very experienced. And in another conversation later on, he told me that the municipal board of the SDS and the Municipal Assembly, the composition of -- the people who were there working as deputies or board members, that their intellectual level was not particularly high. So he asked me, and a number of other intellectuals in Prijedor who were not members of the SDS, to become members -- to become deputies to the assembly. He said they had the statutory right to increase the numbers of deputies in the assembly, and they wanted the ten of us, we were a group of ten people, to join also to help with our professionalism. So we accepted this proposal. And I attended several of the assembly sessions. Unfortunately, this coincided with the time Dr. Stakic was being removed, so tensions were high between the two opposing groups. And whatever was happening in the municipal board of the SDS, what I witnessed myself during that meeting, there were two or maybe even three distinct groups within the SDS. So this rift was reflected during sessions of the assembly. I just didn't think it was worth it for me to join the work of the assembly. So I only went to a couple of sessions, you know, and then I stopped going. We stopped going regularly. And then again, the radical group gained the upper hand in their requests to cut down the number of deputies to the assembly. So we were simply -- we were simply wiped off the list of deputies, and that's how our activity in the assembly came to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is an appropriate time for taking the break. The trial stays adjourned until half past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the Defence may continue immediately when, of course, the witness is in the courtroom, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Your Honour, could I pass on a request. Our scheduling is a little complicated because of Ms. Balaban and what's going on in the Brdjanin case, and we are wondering, specifically Ms. Korner, who was going to cross-examine Ms. Balaban, and has a witness who will be finishing Tuesday afternoon in Brdjanin, whether it's possible we could do a full morning session to 1.45 here, and not have the afternoon. And that would at least give the Defence at least one day next week to meet with their client or go back early. But that is our request for Your Honours to consider if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I was afraid you would come with this. We'll decide it during the break. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we continue, Mr. Krejic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Dr. Milomir Stakic was a member of the people's radical party, Veljko Guberina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Now I know. At the beginning when I first met him, I didn't know that. Later on in conversations, I learned that Dr. Stakic was not a member of the SDS, and that was rather strange, the fact that he had remained the president of the Municipal Assembly when the SDS took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So when you were mentioning the radical part that wanted to remove him from the position of the president of the Municipal Assembly, you didn't mean the radical party?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, no, I meant people who wanted to have the upper hand, who wanted more powerful authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, in one place, you mentioned that Simo proposed that you should occupy a certain position. Since in this case there are several people that we are dealing with with the same name, Simo, who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I meant Simo Miskovic, the president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although you never worked either in the police or in the army, as a person with a degree in law, do you know whether municipal bodies such as the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Board could issue orders either to the army or to the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: They couldn't, no chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you something which I was not aware of when we're talking about Bosanska Krajina. Why was Bosanska Krajina particularly against the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia? What happened after World War II with people from Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Bosanska Krajina and the area of Croatia inhabited mostly by the Serbian population, that is Korbon Banja and Lika, those who were bordering on Bosanska Krajina had a large number of inhabitants who after the Second World War in the years 1946, 1947, and 1948, had been moved to Vojvodina to its parts called Banat, Backa, and Srem. And actually peoples were split, families were split. There were parts of the family who had to move to the parts of Vojvodina which had been liberated by the then people's army, and the other parts of those families had remained behind. So there are very few families, especially among the Serbian population, who don't have relatives in Vojvodina, in Belgrade, and in other larger cities of Serbia. And that is why Bosanska Krajina is very closely connected with Serbia, and to be more precise, with Vojvodina. And that is why the Serbian population from Bosanska Krajina wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain as an integral part of Yugoslavia. That is why even to this very day, ties, special ties are being set up between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, in order to provide for the uninterrupted flow of people who have blood ties, who have family connections. That's one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you, prior to the 1st of May, that is, prior to the 30th of April, left on business to Serbia, how did you return, and why did you return?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I left on the eve of the 1st of May. I had some business that took me there. And on the other hand, my daughter had already been in Novi Sad, and that's why I took the opportunity. We had three days off for the bank holiday of the 1st of May. We didn't work for three days. So I went first to Belgrade, and then to Vojvodina, and I was supposed to return to work, but the connections were interrupted. The roads were not passable between Bosnia and Serbia, so I had to stay on waiting for an opportunity to get back. I couldn't take the car back, but I took a plane from Belgrade to Banja Luka. I had to wait a few days. There were a lot of passengers who wanted to get on that same plane. There was just one plane a day flying from Belgrade to Banja Luka and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you hear? Why were the roads not passable back at the beginning of May throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: When I was on my way to Serbia, on the eve of the 1st of May, I could -- I knew already which parts of the ethnically split country I could go through. There were guards in front of every town, some of the guards were police guards, some of them were mixed guards with the police. And at places, there were also armed people wearing some sorts of uniforms, and those uniforms usually were used for other purposes rather than patrols, but in some places they were worn by the patrols. In front of Tuzla, I was stopped by people wearing uniforms that are -- employees used to wear in the time of national disasters. Those were the civilian protection uniforms. In front of Tuzla, the guards that stopped us wore such uniforms. They had hunting rifles. They pulled over cars. They searched the cars. They inspected our IDs. And after a short discussion, they let us continue because they didn't find anything in our car that they would find disturbing. There were already such tensions that one could smell conflicts in the area. The situation was rather tense, and it forebode war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you returned to Prijedor between April and September 1992, did anything happen to you, any incident involving a police member when you didn't have your driving license on you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a good illustration of the atmosphere that could be felt in the town at the time. I was driving my car, and I didn't have my driving license on. I was not aware of that. I had all the other documents on me. And the policeman stopped me in the night hours. It was around 10.00 in the evening. And since I didn't have my traffic license and driving license, he wanted me to hand over the keys to my car, and I didn't want to do that. And I told him that I would go and get my driving license because I didn't live far from the place where he pulled me over. He allowed me to do that but he didn't allow me to take the car. He asked me to go on foot. When I got back, there was no policeman, and my briefcase was missing from the car. He had taken my briefcase and vanished. I found my briefcase a few days later -- actually, it was a child on the way back from school who found it. It was somewhere cast aside, and the documents were there. But everything else that could be used for general purposes like calculator, pencil, everything else was missing. I complained. On the following day, I called Simo Drljaca, the chief of the public security station whom I knew, and I just wanted to draw his attention to the behaviour of the members of the police. I asked him to check what was going on. And when I told him there was just one policeman, he told me this was not a police patrol, but it was somebody else. He said: "This is not one of my guys." Later on he explained to me that people who had been called up and given reserve police uniforms were still using those uniforms when they go on stealing sprees, when they wanted to rob somebody. And these people were not members of the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Between the 30th of April, 1992, and the end of September 1992, were you aware of the existence of the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Crisis Staff was established?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but I know it was sometime in the month of May, after the takeover of Prijedor. I believe that it was sometime in May that this Crisis Staff was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first half of May, mid-May, the latter part of May?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was in the second -- the latter part of May because I returned from Belgrade on the 8th. So I believe that it was after that, and I really can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with the members of the Crisis Staff once that body was set up?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me right, there was a Crisis Staff, and there was the Executive Board in the Municipal Assembly. So whenever I had contacts with the municipality, it was with the members of the department for finances. I don't know whether Ranko Travar was a member of the Crisis Staff. If he was, then I also had contacts with the Crisis Staff. Ranko Travar was in charge of the finances of the municipality. He was in charge of the financial policies of the Prijedor municipality. And since my institution was also an institution that looked after the financing of the health care in the municipality, I had contacts with Ranko Travar, sometimes with Dr. Kovacevic, and sometimes with Dr. Stakic as physicians who were close to me by the area of their professional activity. And as for the Crisis Staff, as the body of authority, I didn't have any contacts with them because we were an institution which was vertically connected with Banja Luka and with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Travar in his office which belonged to him as a member of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that same apply to Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw each of them in their respective offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you learn about the nature of tasks of the Crisis Staff at the time? Were you at all aware of its activities during its existence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I know it as a person -- as a lawyer. I know what the job of the Crisis Staff is. They do things that pertain to the area of the organisation of the civilian work, what normally pertains to the scope of activities of the municipality is something that the Crisis Staff does in crisis situations. They act independently, and they report to the assembly on their activities. And their job is by and large to create the civilian tasks which pertain to the area of communal activities, the organisation of education, the supply of the population with food, water. So those are all communal activities that I'm referring to. Health care is also one of their activities, but this is only the primary care at the level of the municipality. So all those activities that normally pertain to the area work of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that the Crisis Staff reports to the Municipal Assembly. How often and when?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs are usually set up in the situation when the Municipal Assembly cannot meet. During the periods of crisis, emergency situations, war, other emergency situations such as natural disasters. So that is when the Crisis Staff is set up and becomes active. And according to the regulations, when the conditions are in place for the Municipal Assembly to be called in its full composition, then the Crisis Staff has to offer to the Municipal Assembly the decisions for their approval. So the decisions that the Crisis Staff makes have to be approved by the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you were co-opted or appointed as a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, you know that at that time, Dr. Stakic resigned. That was in January 1993. At the same time, Mr. Simo Drljaca, or on -- or about that time, he stopped being the chief of the public security station in Prijedor. Did Mr. Drljaca -- was he removed or was he promoted? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he went to do something else in Banja Luka. What it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have not yet discussed this as the previous question, either. Did you ever hear that all three political parties in Prijedor made a demand at a session of the Municipal Assembly prior to the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina not to be held at all or that at the very least, it should be postponed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. That was long before the crisis. That was when the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ had a successful cooperation. There was a division of power between the three parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the multiparty elections. And at this time, it was still possible for all the three ethnic national parties to agree that everyone should stay within the same state and live in that state together side by side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name Sead Hrncic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you associate with that name and the period of crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Sead Hrncic was a doctor, a physician, whom I once helped --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you could only tell us his nationality.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. I helped him to come to the hospital in Prijedor and start work there from Sanski Most, which was a place I came from, and to get specialisation in surgery. That's what he wanted. During one period, we would travel together from Sanski Most to Prijedor where we worked. And that's when we became reasonably close friends. At this time, we worked for the same company. Sead appealed to me for help in the period between my return from Belgrade - I can't remember the exact date, but it was between the 10th of May and the 20th of May, roughly speaking. So immediately upon my return from Belgrade, he asked me to talk about a problem that he had. I saw him in my office. That was after work. He told me that certain people, Muslims, had invited him the day before and taken him in a car to a high plateau above Prijedor, to a village that we called Hambarine. They took him there to show him the health station there. I knew that there was indeed a health station in Hambarine. He told me that they had shown him a new health station, and that they were putting equipment for surgery in place at that health station, that they were equipping for all intents and purposes a surgical unit which could be used to perform operations. And they asked him, he said, to be prepared to perform operations in that unit if need should arise or, in other words, if conflict broke out as was already expected between the Muslims forces and the army. He told me that when he went to Hambarine, he passed a number of armed guards that Muslims had set up in order to secure the area. He wanted my advice. He asked me what he should do. He was scared, shocked. His wife was a Croat. They had two small children. He asked my advice. He said: "What should I do?" He was scared because he did not have many alternatives. He was scared to remain in Prijedor, because what would become of him unless he complied with the requests that those people had made of him. He was afraid for his family. And yet, on the other hand, he was not prepared to cooperate with those people who were in a sense paramilitary units. I told him: "You don't have much choice. You should go and report this to the relevant bodies." And I was referring first and foremost to military bodies, because we were, after all, talking about armed units, armed groups of people. I said: "Your only alternative is to leave this area." He was not from Sanski Most originally, but from Kljuc. Kljuc is a small town 30 kilometres from Sanski Most. I told him that it would be best for him to leave and go to his -- stay with his family there or go to another place where he would be safe. And then after we had this talk, he gave me another call. He had spoken to his wife, and they agreed -- they had agreed to leave for Croatia, to stay with his wife's relatives. He asked for my help to go to Belgrade because you couldn't go to Croatia at that point. So he wanted to go to Belgrade, to Serbia, through -- and then try to reach Croatia through Hungary, via Hungary, which he eventually did. I secured him a plane ticket from Banja Luka for Belgrade, and he left with his wife and two children. At a later time, he called me, he got in touch with me from somewhere around Vienna, and I think he still lives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Krejic. This concludes our examination-in-chief, and now you will be questioned by my colleague from the Prosecution and probably finally also by the Honourable Chamber. Thank you, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this concrete and fast line of questions and answers. And I hope we can proceed in the same now when you are facing the questions put to you by the OTP. Ms. Sutherland, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, you mentioned in your earlier testimony refugees coming from Croatia into Bosnia. Were the refugees coming into all the towns in the Bosanska Krajina including Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I think so. I know more about the towns where I used to stay, and I'm talking about the four towns which are part of my region: Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Sanski Most, and Prijedor. But I think many people did go to Banja Luka, yes, in view of the fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And they went to Banja Luka town, the city of Banja Luka itself?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, mainly, people would go wherever their relatives were, if any. Usually they would stay with their relatives. So if the relatives were in a village, they would go to a village. If they were in town, they would go to that particular town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit SK49, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I'll give you a moment to look at that document, and then I'd like to take you to a portion of it. This is a document entitled "notebook of minutes from the meetings of the coordinating body of the Prijedor SDS municipal board for 1992." And it's dated February 1992. Could I ask you to turn to the page which has a number at the top of it, P0041689.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And for Your Honours and the Defence, it's on page 4 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I may ask the usher to put this page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, do you see Simo Drljaca's name in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can read that through together --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you bring me the document, usher, I will show you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we read through this together, I then have a question for you. So under Simo Drljaca's name, it says, does it not, "who will prepare the administrative organs of the Serbian Municipal Assembly." And then it goes on: "The president of the Prijedor Serbian Municipal Assembly has been entrusted with coming up with a proposal for forming a government and departments of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality by 1400 hours on Thursday, 16th of April, 1992." It then reads: "Miskovic and two councilmen had to come up with nominations for the SDP, SDK, the bank, and the court. Drljaca and Radovan Krejic have been appointed coordinators. [Stakic, Savanovic, and Baltic were entrusted with all preparations for the Serbian Assembly]. And Simo Drljaca and Radovan Krejic were appointed the coordinators." Sir, that paragraph I have just read to you, was that in preparation for the takeover of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Two requests for interruption. First, the Defence, and then from the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Only my learned friend skipped in the first line two letters, IO, meaning Executive Board, or Izvrsni Odbor. So it's not Municipal Assembly; it's Executive Board of Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the question from the side of the Judges was: Do you intend to continue with the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you then be so kind and to read out also the next lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Continuing from where I left off, i.e., that Simo Drljaca and yourself had been appointed as coordinators, the document then reads: "Milovan Dragic will provide the premises, and Ranko Nikic will provide security for the premises." The document then reads: "Stakic" and under his name, "the information commission should make a statement regarding information about the occurrences." Sir, my question is, that paragraph that I have just read to you, is that in relation to preparations for the takeover of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: This is completely new on me. It's the first time I see it. I was not aware that I was holding a position of any kind of coordinator, believe me. This may be just a proposal that was made, but I was certainly never informed of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Even though you're seeing the document today for the first time, do you have an opinion as to whether this was in preparation for the takeover of the Serbian municipality -- of the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can consider this now, but I was really not informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you to consider it now. Reading that paragraph, "the president of the Prijedor Serbian assembly Executive Board has been entrusted with coming up with a proposal for forming a government and departments of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality." And then Simo Drljaca and yourself were appointed as coordinators. And Stakic, Savanovic, and Baltic, were entrusted with all the preparations for the Serbian Assembly. What is your opinion on that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say anything by just looking at a single page without knowing what this was really about and why these things were Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 10577 to 10586. being considered. I was never at any point in time informed of being appointed a coordinator of anything. I was in Belgrade in those days officially -- on official business.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The date of this meeting was the 13th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I never attended a meeting like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you went to Belgrade on the eve of the 30th of May [sic], 1992 --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, on the eve of the 1st of May or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think you said you returned around the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Around the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many days were you absent from work?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Between the 1st and the 8th, except that we had three days off at that time. It was an official holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move now to another topic. We can -- I have finished with the document that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to present the document both in English and B/C/S to the Judges, please. Thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, you mentioned a gentleman Sead Cikota in your testimony earlier today. Did you sign his dismissal notice dated the 1st of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: If it was part of all the dismissal notices, well, then, it may have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many dismissal notices did you sign?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I signed the dismissal notices of all those who had been absent from work more than they were then allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know why Sead Cikota had been absent from work?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I later found out when I heard that he had been taken to an investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that he was taken -- he was imprisoned in Omarska briefly, and he was released after a period of time because he was proven innocent. Are you aware that Sead Cikota was detained in Omarska from the 30th of May until the 6th of August, 1992, after the foreign journalists had visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I got to know about his being taken away when his wife told me about it. I knew that he was over there. I didn't know when he would be released or when he was released, but I found out from a friend. I've mentioned that he was in Trnopolje, and that's when we went over to Trnopolje to visit him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So your visit to the Trnopolje camp was after the 6th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
