utterances.text: When I received word that he was there, I can't remember the dates, that's when we went to see him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that his wife told you that he was -- had been put on a bus and taken to Omarska. Do you know what happened --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, no, she didn't say how. She just told me that she was in Omarska. She didn't say how she got there, by bus or in a different way. She just told me that she was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think it's my fault. Sead Cikota's wife told you that he was in the camp, and that's when you went to speak to Simo Drljaca about trying to get him out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, she said that he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to his wife, Zlata Cikota?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Now, I do. But then, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That she was arrested on the 23rd of June at their home and taken to the SUP, and then taken from there to the Omarska camp where she was detained for 42 days?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard this from Sead when he came later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know why she was arrested?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know that Zlata Cikota was chairperson of the referendum election committee for the independent Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. I knew that she was a member of the SDA. Her husband told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you aware of any crimes committed by either Sead Cikota or his wife Zlata?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to proceed with this line of questions related to Mr. Sead Cikota. Did I understand it correctly that you said that the fact that a person was detained, in this case, in Omarska, for a certain period of time, and therefore not reporting to work, is a reason for dismissal?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: All institutions in Prijedor, and all companies, were informed that all those who were supposed to respond to the mobilisation callup but failed to do so and failed to appear, to show up for work on that particular day should be dismissed. And we followed this instruction. So we were only trying to find out on the basis of records who was missing. We didn't try to find out the reasons. And all those who had no justification for having been absent for five days were automatically dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But when you learned from Mr. Cikota's wife that he was detained in Omarska, did you rethink your decision of dismissal of Mr. Cikota? Was it when you knew about the reasons why he didn't show up at work --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was reason enough to dismiss, and to let him be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I did rethink the whole thing then. But as he was already at the investigation centre, and that he was being investigated, and the police had promised me that the investigation would be sped up in order to find out the truth as quickly as possible, I waited for notification by the police to see whether any criminal proceedings would be started against him or whether he would be released. As he was finally released, and he came to Prijedor, he also came to see me. And I told him that he could get back to work. But even when we met in Trnopolje, he told me that his intention was to leave the country together with his family. So he did have a possibility to continue working since it was proven that he was blameless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you then please tell us when it was that you visited Mr. Cikota in the Trnopolje centre? Was he there alone, or together with his wife?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I visited him, I think it was a day or two days later after he came to Trnopolje from Omarska. After I found out from my friends that he was in Trnopolje, we drove over to see him, and I believed that we might be able to bring him back home because Trnopolje was a collection centre from which you could leave and go home. I found him surrounded by several other people from Prijedor. It was some sort of a makeshift tent. People used blankets to put up these tents. It was summer. It was quite hot, and they were sitting outside this makeshift tent. They had built a fire, and they were eating something. They were grilling some meat when we came. They even had drinks, and they offered us drinks. His wife was not with him. I think -- I'm not sure, but I think that he didn't at that point know where his wife was. I certainly didn't know. We talked, and I offered him a lift back to Prijedor. And then he told me that there were a number of formalities, unfinished formalities with the administration there, with the people keeping the records in the camp. And this was in the afternoon. It was about 5.00, 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon when we were there. So he had to stay for another day so that during regular working hours, he could get his papers straight. He had applied before for permission to leave the country. And he said he would stay another day to get the paperwork done, and as soon as that was over and done with, he would call me. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us that you visited Simo Drljaca in order to intervene in the interest of Sead Cikota. Where did you meet Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: In his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And his office was located where at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: In the secretariat for the interior, in the same place where the office of the chief of the public security station still is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have from this discussion the impression that Simo Drljaca had, in fact, the possibility to intervene whether or not a person was detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I had the impression that he could intervene, although he explained to me that his interference was not welcome, that his involvement was not welcome, because there are investigative bodies whose duties is to verify the facts, and when the facts are verified and known, then, he would be able to do what I asked him to do, to help and speed up the process of releasing Sead Cikota in case it was proven that he wasn't involved in any criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you also try to contact other persons in Prijedor in order to end this detention or deprivation of liberty of Mr. Cikota?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I talked to Dr. Stakic about that as well. As I knew him and Dr. Kovacevic as doctors, I talked to Dr. Stakic, and he referred me to the police and the military [as interpreted]. They told me to go there because it is there that I would be able to possibly achieve what I wanted to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the order was you went first to Dr. Stakic, and he then asked you to go to Simo Drljaca. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: First I went to Dr. Kovacevic. I knew him better because we had worked together for a longer time. I didn't know Dr. Stakic as well as I knew Dr. Kovacevic. But I went to see them more because of the fact that I knew them as physicians. I knew that their authority was not as broad in scope as it could be. But they could tell me where to go. That was the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I also ask, where did you visit Mr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic, in which building?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: In the building of the municipality where their offices were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this was following your testimony after the 8th of May. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you. After the 8th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of May, when you returned to Prijedor, as you told us previously.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic wear at that time uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Dr. Kovacevic wore a pair of blue jeans. Actually, I didn't go to Dr. Stakic's office. I went to Dr. Kovacevic's office. And Dr. Kovacevic wore a pair of blue jeans. That's what I remember because he didn't wear blue jeans very often. No, I didn't see them wearing uniforms at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said you didn't go to Dr. Stakic's office. Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I believe that the two of us went to Dr. Kovacevic's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would mean -- sorry, I'm a little bit confused today. But this would once again mean that first you contacted Dr. Stakic, and then, as you said, "the two of us went to Dr. Kovacevic's office." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Wrong translation. Wrong translation. The witness didn't say "we went," but "we were" there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I'll explain. It's not a problem. I went to see Dr. Kovacevic, because I knew him much better. And it was early in the morning. Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic were together in the office, in Dr. Kovacevic's office, and they were having their morning coffee. I had a cup of coffee with them. I made -- I asked what I wanted to know. We talked about the situation in the health-care system. And then I went to Simo Drljaca, not on the same day. I could not arrange for an appointment on the same day. I had to make an appointment for the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So why did you believe that Dr. Kovacevic could have any influence on the detention of Mr. Cikota? In which capacity did you visit Dr. Kovacevic, and then meeting at the same time Dr. Stakic there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I was very close with Dr. Kovacevic, as we had worked in the same institution for a number of years. And I would visit him in his office from time to time, mostly to talk to him about the situation in the health-care system. And since I didn't have any information on what was going on with the police, with the army, and the investigation centre or prison as they called it, then I used that opportunity to ask him. He also knew Cikota, and I thought that maybe with his help, I would have more influence on the person who could actually help Cikota to get home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who were the most influential people and persons in -- at that time in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the political influence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I believe that the biggest political influence was exerted by Mr. Srdjo Srdic immediately prior to the war, because he was a deputy and president of the SDS. So I believe that his was the strongest political influence. Dr. Kovacevic had the authority, but not so much the political authority. He was an influential person by the virtue of his personality. He was a popular person and a doctor who was held in high esteem. And I believe that Dr. Kovacevic had the strongest personal influence as a doctor. And Mr. Srdjo Srdic had the biggest political influence as a politician. I'm talking about the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about the influence of Dr. Stakic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the political influence of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I have already said that he didn't have a huge political influence because he was very young at the time. He was rather unknown in town. He had just completed his university education, and he worked in an outpatient surgery was not located in town. So very few people knew him at the time. In our practice, people who were in executive positions have a lot more influence than those who preside over the assembly because the assembly is a collective body of power which makes decision on general issues, passes regulations, so it doesn't have the executive power. So that's why it is not so much in the spotlight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But wasn't it, when you make this assessment, a surprise for you that first he was elected vice-president and later became president?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't surprised. I think it was sheer inertia. As a Serb, he was the only person in any office in the assembly, and he inherited, so to say, the position of the president. Dr. Kovacevic was in the highest executive office, while Muhamed was still presiding over the assembly. And Dr. Stakic was not so much in the spotlight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have good contacts with Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Until the conflict that I spoke about, the misunderstanding that we had, I had excellent contacts with Mr. Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know about the fate of Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Now I do. I was with his family. We are neighbours. We live in the same town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what did you learn and what did you learn about the reasons, and what is your own assessment of this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I did not hear any details. The family didn't give me too many details. They told me that he had a tragic end during the investigation procedure when he was incarcerated. He didn't return. They are not aware of any details of his death. They only told me that he met his end during the investigation. And the reasons: The reasons are the same that led up to this war. The causes of the war are the same causes that resulted in the suffering of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever intervene in the interest of other persons you knew at that time, for example, in the interest of Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I didn't. When Mr. Cehajic was arrested, I spoke to his wife who was my colleague at work. She is a doctor. And she was the assistant CEO at the hospital. We worked together for a number of years. And she came to my place to tell me what was going on. And in that conversation, we concluded -- she even told me that it would be -- that it was safer for Mr. Cehajic to be in the prison. Maybe not in the prison, but that he was sort of put away because there was a danger for him. He was a prominent leader of the SDA belonging to the Muslim body of the population. There was a danger that the entire family would suffer at the hand of people who instigated some incidents. And Mrs. Cehajic concluded that maybe it was the best for the entire situation because the possible guilt or innocence of her husband would be proven. We still thought that the situation would not end up in any serious conflicts, and that the whole situation would be terminated in a professional way by learning the real truth about all these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are speaking about guilt or innocence. What was the alleged crime Mr. Cehajic had committed that gave reason to detain him from liberty and incarcerate him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: There were some indications that within the Muslim population, forces were being prepared. That's why I gave you the example of Dr. Hrncic, that paramilitary formations were being established in some parts of Prijedor Municipality, and even broader, in the general area of Prijedor. There were such cases in other places as well, in my town, Sanski Most, and in its vicinity. Paramilitary units had already been formed. Muslims were being armed, and it was already a public secret. And there were some indications that some prominent high-ranking officials who worked in Prijedor Municipality had participated in the illegal arming of parts of the Muslim people and the establishment of paramilitary formations which eventually might cause some armed conflicts. There were later on some incidents, skirmishes, exchanges of fire. And I believe that that was the reason for instigating investigations, in order to establish who among the Muslim officials participated in the formation of these paramilitary units. To my mind, that was the reason. And also, when I exchanged views with Muslims who were outside of the reach of these investigations, we believed that that was the reason, and that a professional investigation would eventually show who were the ones who had to be investigated and who were the ones who were innocent of that allegation and that the latter ones would then be liberated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Krejic, until now, I really could follow your decent testimony. But here, I'm afraid I can't follow you. You knew Mr. Cehajic as the president at that time, and Dr. Stakic was deputy. And you knew that the follower of Mr. Cehajic was Dr. Stakic. Did you really believe that this honest person, as you yourself characterised him, would be part of these activities as you told us of Muslim people and the establishment of paramilitary formations? Did you really believe this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I have told you when the Defence counsel asked me that I worked one floor above the headquarters of the SDA. Straight below me was Mr. Mirza Mujadzic's office, and we had daily political activities. And I found myself in the situation to see a number of Muslim activists in that party who were armed already at the time when nobody could foresee that the things that would later on happen would really happen. Mirza Mujadzic also came to work carrying arms. His escorts as well. Mr. Muhamed Cehajic came to these premises almost on a daily basis. After Sead Hrncic told me what he told me, and I trusted him, I could assume that there was hardly anybody who was not involved. In other words, there's a possibility that everybody was involved in the activities that led up to the war. And since the situation escalated very rapidly, I was inclined to believe that there were good enough reasons to establish the responsibility of every single person; at the same time, I believe that those who were innocent would be set free, and that they wouldn't have any harm becoming to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the fate of Mr. Cehajic together with Dr. Stakic who had apparently a close connection to and with Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have an opportunity to discuss that with him. It was the time when you couldn't really talk about the destiny of these people. We all believed that these people would return very quickly. All I know about the destiny of people who suffered in one way or another I learned after the war when Muslims started returning to Prijedor and Sanski Most, when I met up with them again. They talked to me openly because I had then - I still have - a lot of Muslim friends. So I actually learned from them all those things that are now known about the events that had taken place in those investigation centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Two short additional questions: Did you ever see Madam Plavsic in Prijedor, or did you participate in a meeting together with her, maybe in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No. The only SDS official I saw is Mr. Krajisnik. He attended a session which I attended as well. I believe that he was invited, or maybe he was there just by accident, when we discussed the conflict between Dr. Stakic and the others who asked for his resignation. And I believe that Mr. Krajisnik at that time attended a session of the assembly. I never saw Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You gave us deep insight in that what happened in Prijedor today. What is your assessment? Was the situation as it developed later planned and elaborated on the level of Prijedor, or did the politically responsible persons in Prijedor rely on orders given from a higher level, whatever this level may be?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I can just tell you what I think, because I'm not aware of all the facts. My opinion is -- has changed or has developed. At the beginning, I was inclined to believe that whatever was happening was organised and masterminded from a centre, because similar things were happening in many municipalities. I thought that this was following a scenario. But as the war went on, it appeared that people acted the same or in a similar way in the same situation, in a similar situation. It was more of a chaos than an organised situation. So when I look back on that situation, I think that the situation that all of us faced dictated the development of events. That is my impression.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you take other opportunities to visit Dr. Stakic in the period between the 8th of May and the end of September 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: In his office, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Both in his office, in his apartment, or in Omarska, wheresoever.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: We did see each other -- I don't know how many times, but usually in my office. You know, Dr. Stakic would sometimes surprise me by dropping by to my office. Dr. Kovacevic used to come and see me in my office very frequently. They would sometimes drop by for a medical issue, over a medical issue, if there was a patient being treated they wanted to have a look at the medical records. So it was more in their professional capacity as doctors, rather than as politicians. So we would usually see each other in my office, but always in relation to some medical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic ever express that he had difficulties with his job as you in the beginning mentioned that from your point of view, you would have appreciated if he would have stayed in the health area? Did you ever discuss this -- did Dr. Stakic ever complain about orders he received or the lack of responsibility or the lack of influence or complaining about the development he saw in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: In all my conversations with Dr. Stakic, throughout that period, I got the impression that he was dissatisfied with the way the army treated him. I'm not sure only him, but he wasn't satisfied with the way the army related to the entire organisation of Prijedor Municipality. He said that the army was taken up and using up far too much of the human resources, and that very few people stayed behind to organise the economy. Many people from our own services and institutions, and I'm talking about medical services and medical institutions, and most of the people working there were women, but many people were in the service of the military medical corps and medical units. He and Dr. Kovacevic often told me there was no way for them to make sure that the economy in the town worked because too many people had been taken somewhere else and on military duties. So in those conversations, my impression was that he was unhappy with the situation, and that was precisely what led me to advise him to leave politics behind and to return to his job as a doctor, especially in view of his young age. I said: "You're so young. There will still be plenty of time for you to go back to politics."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that Dr. Stakic was in agreement with the development in Prijedor, especially those developments leading to the setting up of camps like Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't think he was in agreement. I think as a human being, what really bothered him the most is that there was a camp located exactly in the area from which he came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss with him the question whether or not in his political function he would have influence to overcome this deplorable situation and to take care that as soon as possible, these camps would no longer exist?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what influence he could exert really. He was not in a position to exert any influence, I think, for the job being done in the investigation centres to be done as quickly as possible. But I think he would have been in favour of that, and he would have favoured going back to life as normal as quickly as possible, especially in view of the economic situation in Prijedor. Those were difficult times. It was very difficult to supply the population with everything they needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But what about the economic situation in comparison to the -- to that what I think is now undisputed, killing of thousands of people on the territory of the Municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, you mean the possibility of using manpower for the economic activities that were underway in the investigation centres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Balancing the problems. You mentioned the problem, no doubt, that there were enormous economic problems in the municipality of Prijedor, but especially for persons having sworn an oath as doctors to take care of human beings, that on the territory of the Municipality of Prijedor, he was - Dr. Stakic - was the president of the Municipal Assembly, that on this territory where he had some - I emphasise "some" - political responsibility, that there happened these what we now call crimes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question. Was this a question or a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is what was more in the centre of your discussions, the economic difficulties or the fact that there were these Detention Centres, these camps in the municipality of Prijedor, and allegedly there were committed as it is alleged now more than thousands of killings of innocent persons? What was more in the centre of your discussions with Dr. Stakic, the economic situation or this problem to the centre of human life?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: When I spoke with Dr. Stakic, and particularly with Dr. Kovacevic, I discussed the situation in our health system. You know, whenever I had an opportunity to meet up with them, I would use the opportunity because they were very busy during that period in their jobs. So I couldn't see them that often. So every time I could, I used the opportunity to appeal to them for assistance. I'm talking about financial assistance and assistance in terms of equipment because a lot of humanitarian aid was coming in. So I insisted that they use their influence with the humanitarian organisations to give as much aid as possible to the health organisations. So of course, I also tried to use our contact to get the material and equipment used to treat people medically, in the hospital in Prijedor as well as outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then there were other issues concerning the local economy, which was only a consequence of the economic situation. Whenever they explained that they were not really in a position to do much to help the health institutions, they would speak about the economy, about the local economy. I'm not into economics myself, but that's why we talked about it, the economy, because the state of the local economy was the reason why we couldn't get more money and more aid for the health organisation. And we didn't discuss anything else, especially not the investigation centres, because we only knew precious little about it at that point. Most of what I learned about the investigation centres, I learned only after the war from Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know it's time for the break, but really only a short answer. Did you ever meet Dr. Stakic wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I can't remember right now. I cannot completely rule out the possibility that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a certain period of time --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I know that he wore a hat during the war. So I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a certain period of time where more or less all or the majority of the civil staff wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed. Once - I think it was sent by the secretariat for National Defence, I got information that we were all supposed to wear uniforms, and they meant the directors and the heads of organisations. And I bought a uniform from a certain company which I kept in my cupboard. The first day I wore a uniform myself, but later on when I saw no one was asking questions why I wasn't wearing a uniform, I just left it in my cupboard and that's where it stayed for the whole duration of the war. I think the secretariat for National Defence did send us a note, because there was a work obligation that we were supposed to wear a uniform at work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate when -- at what point in time this was? Apparently, it must have been after the 8th of May. Was it close to the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me? That was much later. I think it may have even been as late as 1993 when the serious mobilisation began and the war was getting serious. But it was not back then, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's now time to have the break. But before the break, I want to ask, please be prepared after the break, when we have finalised the testimony, we have to discuss the questions for next Monday and some related issues. The trial stays adjourned until 5.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. As regards now the first question by the Prosecution, on Tuesday, I think we have really to act spontaneously, and nobody can now predict how long the witness will take us that day. And I think we have to stick to the schedule as foreseen, and there are three strong representatives of the Prosecution, therefore we are not afraid at all that we can continue. And at this point in time, in fact, we do not know what really will be heard that Wednesday. So it would be premature to decide on this today. And sometimes we have to stick to the schedule. It has to be a reliable schedule; also the Judges have some other commitments, office commitments and office duties. And therefore, I apologise, but it's not possible to rearrange the schedule. Thank you for coming again, Mr. Krejic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko has some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, can I ask you to explain why Dr. Stakic, a young, unknown doctor, as you said, was elected as vice-president and then president of the Municipal Assembly and then appointed as the president of the Crisis Staff while such political figures as Srdjo Srdic, Simo Miskovic, Milan Kovacevic were ignored, let us say?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is my own opinion. It's really difficult to know for sure. But I assume that the more experienced ones used a younger person to put him in a situation where he was not so much at ease. Sometimes, you know, it's due to the circumstances that you have a situation in which someone ends up where they least expect themselves to end up. In Serbia these days, we have a president now, a lady president, who had only been in politics prior to that for a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You testified today that radical part of the SDS leadership decided to remove Dr. Stakic from his position in the autumn of 1992. Can you specify, what was -- what were the differences between Dr. Stakic's position, I mean, attitude and stance, and more radical members of SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: My impression was that the radical group, the people we keep referring to as the radical wing inside the SDS, was dissatisfied by the fact that Mr. Stakic, as the president of the Crisis Staff and the president of the Municipal Assembly, was not enough of a hardliner. They thought he should show more determination, wield his power more, so that he could put up the various forces that were, so to speak, not under the control of the administration, armed forces, including also police forces. I know that once when I attended a meeting of the Municipal Assembly, as what I refer to as co-opted member, there was a request to call the leaders of the armed forces to explain before the assembly what they were asking themselves about, what people in the town were asking themselves. So those deputies were requested to somehow to put up a stand to the military authorities. I suppose Dr. Stakic failed to do so. He was not successful. I'm not sure why, or perhaps he didn't even try. Maybe he thought that was the outside of the scope of the civilian authorities. Now, why they demanded that he should do it, I suppose only they really know. But that was the impression you got when you sat there and listened to their discussion at the assembly session. I think even a conclusion was reached for the commanders to be called before the assembly and to have them explain why they were mobilising so many people and why they were mobilising so many people from Prijedor town itself, and that that should be stopped because they were taking and using up too many people for the armed forces. I think that was probably the reason they thought that Dr. Stakic was not aggressive enough, not wielding his power enough. And they thought that by continuing to work the way he was working, he would not have been able to increase the power of the civilian authorities in the town of Prijedor. And their position was, I suppose, that he should have worked in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So Dr. Stakic was in position to influence military and police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I suppose that he was not in a position to influence them just for the very fact that he did not influence them. I don't think he had influence. I'm only saying that the radical group believed that there should be more influence, and that he was incapable of exerting the influence or that perhaps he was not willing to exert such influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You said you advised Dr. Stakic to quit politics and go back working as a doctor. What was the reaction of Dr. Stakic on your advice?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I think those were exactly the days when he resigned. It was toward the end of 1992 when I went to the assembly a couple of times, and I had opportunity to talk to him in my office. I'm not sure how much I influenced his decision, but I think very soon after that, he retired from politics. It was in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the last question: How and when you became aware that Dr. Stakic was a member of the national or people's radical party established by Veljko Guberina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I learned this at the time when there was the debate on the removal of Dr. Stakic from his position as the president of the Municipal Assembly. The radical group used as one its arguments the fact that Dr. Stakic was not a member of the SDS. They gave this as their reason, as the reason for their attempt to have the president of the Municipal Assembly removed. That was the first time I heard about that. I wasn't involved in the foundation and establishment of the people's radical party, but that was the first time I heard that Dr. Stakic was actually not a member of the SDS. Later on, when I got to know him better and he became the head of the health centre, so we talked more often, it was then that I learned about the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you have any idea about the platform of the people's radical party, Guberina people's radical party?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I don't. But I can assume what it was, because I've seen several political platforms from the time before the war, and they were all identical. They all had as one of the principal aims the taking of power, and the idealogical differences between these different platforms were insignificant. I looked at the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ political platforms, and let me tell you, I would put my signature under any of though platforms, even now, even today, but unfortunately it turned out later that no one really adhered to those platforms. Those platforms were mere declarations of intentions, but what they really wanted to do was grab power, all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I think you were telling us that when your colleague or the person who was working with you was taken to Omarska to be interrogated, and then you went to see Mr. Drljaca to ask and try to help him, that you were sort of expecting a trial or a procedure just to know if a person was guilty or innocent, I suppose, because of your legal training. And do you know of any procedure going on in Prijedor at that time against any of the detainees in the Omarska camp? Not only your friend or your colleague, but other people.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I didn't know at that time what was going on in Omarska. It was very difficult to know for us who were removed from that situation. But I later found out that investigations had been carried out in Omarska, and that some of the documents -- and that the documents were preserved. But as far as I know, criminal reports were never filed against any of the persons who had been investigated, at least not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Did you know, as a lawyer, who was the president of the court in Prijedor at the time of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Again, much later, I found out that he was one of the victims. But I only found out about this later, after the war, when people who had been in Omarska returned from abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Did you know some of the judges in the judiciary of Prijedor at the time of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And were they dismissed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know who was dismissed, if any of them. But most of them stayed in their positions, those who were there before the war, during the war, and after the war. And they are still in their positions. They still hold the same posts, but I couldn't give you any of the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And do you know of some of the judges and the prosecutors who were taken to Omarska also?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I only know about Seric. I don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you think the people who worked in the judiciary at the time of the takeover and that they stay, and you say that some of them are still holding the same offices, that they tried to start criminal proceedings against one of these persons, detainees, in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about any such proceedings. I really don't know. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now for the Defence. Additional questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only one question, as a follow-up question of a question of the Honourable Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that Mr. Stakic had been removed by the radical group within the SDS because he failed to impose his authority on the army and the police. What is your opinion? This new group, were they successful in imposing their authority on the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: As I've said, the impression was, by listening to the debates during sessions of the assembly and at meetings of the municipal board once, the group was dissatisfied with Dr. Stakic's lack of determination. They thought that the position he held should have been used to better effect to influence certain activities and change things in favour of the administration. But it turned out later that the situation did not change much after Dr. Stakic's removal. I think the armed forces and the police forces, and the TO forces were a world unto themselves, and the civilian authorities could do nothing to influence their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krejic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, Judge Argibay asked you questions about the judiciary in Prijedor. Can you tell the Court the names of the Muslim and Croat judges who remained in their positions after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about their ethnicity. I know that a number of judges have remained. I knew very few judges personally. I knew the president of the court since as in my capacity as director of the health insurance fund, my contacts were with heads of various departments, and he was the one who was in charge of the judiciary administration and he was the one who was familiar with the laws in the area of health insurance. I knew very few judges personally. I wouldn't come across them in the court, if I came to the court. I believe that Muslims left from the court like they did from all the other institutions. I don't know any Muslims who have remained. I knew very few of them anyway. I only knew one lawyer. They are the two lawyers that I knew. They have left Prijedor, but now they have returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly had the power to set the agenda; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: The agenda of the session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they put their agenda together. I really was not in the position to see how the agenda was established for the Municipal Assembly. I attended only two or three sessions of the assembly, and I had been given the agenda. It was usually the secretary of the assembly who prepared the agenda, and then he would send it to the president of the assembly who would then read it. This was then documented in the minutes, and it was adopted by the assembly. How the agenda was prepared by the secretariat in the assembly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the agenda of the two or three sessions that attended, was there ever discussion about the camps, the cleansing of the Muslim villages or crimes committed against the Muslim or Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Futher questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One final question: From your point of view, who was higher ranking in the Crisis Staff of Prijedor from the persons you knew very well, Simo Drljaca, Mr. Kovacevic, or Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're referring to. In legal terms, the president, given his position, should be more important. But if you are referring to the real authority that people had, I believe that Simo Drljaca had the highest authority, and that Dr. Kovacevic commanded the most respect in the Crisis Staff. But in legal terms, it was Dr. Stakic who was the president. So that would be their ranking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In legal terms, would it have been possible for Dr. Stakic to give orders to one of the other two persons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN KREJIC
utterances.text: Not to Simo Drljaca. Simo Drljaca was appointed following a different procedure. He was in the MUP, in the then SUP, and the situation there is similar like in the health-insurance fund. There was a vertical hierarchy from the municipality up to the republic. And I believe that the person that Simo Drljaca reported to was in Banja Luka, and Dr. Kovacevic had the executive function. He was in the -- and he presided over the executive body. So there was no subordination between them. Dr. Stakic, as the president of the assembly, should have insisted on the implementation of the decisions passed by the assembly. So the Crisis Staff should have implemented these decisions or returned them for review to the municipality if they thought that there was no legal foundation for the implementation of such decisions. The president of the municipality cannot give orders to the Executive Board. It's an independent body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any further questions? I can't see any. Thank you very much for coming, and thank you for your time, and thank you for giving us your testimony with a lot of new insight and that what happened in 1992 in Prijedor. And have a safe and good return to Prijedor. Thank you very much for coming once again. You're excused for today. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope I have contributed for you to finding the real truth about the events in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we now turn to the question of Monday's witnesses. The Defence is prepared, insisting, or whatsoever hearing Mr. Mujadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we want to thank the Court and the OTP for giving us an opportunity to meet and visit with our client, as we did so this morning. And there were some things that we did discuss that we would like to share with the Court relating to the specific question the Court raised. At this time, although we're somewhat perplexed as to the procedures involved in questioning or opening the questioning for Mr. Murselovic, Mr. Sivac, and Dr. Mujadzic, quite frankly, we're a bit respectfully chagrined that the OTP has an opportunity to open their case, to ask questions, to submit new evidence, and to continue to establish things that they either failed or didn't expect at one point to present. After consulting with the Defence team, including our consultation with Dr. Stakic, we are of the opinion, despite the fact that there were those six late disclosures pursuant to Rule 68, in light of the fact that there seems to be a rush to conclude certain witnesses, that we will not be asking Dr. Mujadzic any further questions, other than that which we've asked during our initial cross-examination. And will not be supplementing our cross-examination of Dr. Mujadzic. We would like, when the time is appropriate, to address two other points with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it that on Monday morning, we start immediately with the next witness in line. This would be, if I'm not wrong, 040. The witness had previously testified in the Omarska case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, please, the other issues you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was an issue raised by the OTP with respect to Mr. Mayhew who is an OTP witness who testified. There has been some correspondence from the OTP which identifies certain documents that were available to the witness during his testimony and during the cross-examination, as well as part of the redirect. It was revealed that he may, if he had just done a cursory review of his file or his computer that he would have come up with critical information that purportedly he was relying on but didn't give during his testimony. Although, personally I was lectured about corresponding to people and individuals in writing, we, the Defence, were never informed in writing despite the parametres being set by the OTP that Mr. Mayhew would appear and is willing to retestify. It's a separate issue from the Rule 68 disclosures. We do not expect based upon the Court's comments upon reviewing Mr. Mayhew's testimony, based upon the Court's deliberations and judicial hints that were offered to us in connection with Mr. Mayhew's testimony, discussing it with Dr. Stakic, and relying upon the Court's comments during his testimony as well as the comments of the Court during the deliberations and the judicial hints, we likewise will not be seeking to open and supplement our cross-examination of Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After deliberation, accepted. Next issue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next issue involves actually the witnesses that were identified to us under what we categorise the Rule 68 statements and disclosures. The Court has invited us, it's my recollection, invited us to seek assistance from the Court as to which witnesses we would like the Court to subpoena or assist in bringing here. We have consulted and believe that with the Court's permission, we can share the name of two of those individuals. But again, taking the most precaution, perhaps I should identify their names in private session, if necessary. But I'll proceed in the manner in which the Court desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have already on the transcript in open session discussed these names. So I can't see a reason why we should go into private session for this purpose. So if you could be so kind and to address these names, and then also to specify whether you want us to subpoena these persons or whether you have good reasons that you asked the Court to call these witnesses as Chamber witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To answer the two-fold question is is it's at the Court's discretion if the Court wishes to subpoena or to grant us a subpoena to come here. We were informed by these witnesses that they will not, because of their understanding, having given statements and interviews with the OTP, will not be cooperating with the Defence. Because, namely, some of them are either suspects or believe that they will be suspects in future or sealed indictments. So they are not cooperating with us, but are cooperating and have cooperated, given that they have provided those interviews, with the OTP. We believe that the issue of the Crisis Staff, the authority within this Crisis Staff is relevant and is quite frankly important for the understanding in order to adjudicate any facts, much less applying the law to this case. Therefore, we would respectfully suggest that the witnesses, should the Court decide to call them, be limited to those witnesses that were members of the Crisis Staff or allegedly members of the Crisis Staff. I'm not sure if the Court has read in complete their statements. And that would include Ranko Travar, Mr. Pavicic, and Slavko Budimir. Of those three -- or, in the alternative, respectfully, the Court, again, with your discretion, we believe at the very least, two of those three may assist us in coming to a just result in this case and having a better understanding of the circumstances and events that unfolded in Prijedor and Bosnia in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask the Prosecution for comments on this. But please, take already now into account that apparently, it seems to be a waste of time to subpoena these persons in case they don't want to appear as witnesses for the Defence. So it would save time, in fact, that they would appear as Chamber witnesses. One prerequisite, once again, would be the balancing of the interests of the victims against the interests of Defence and the interests of justice of coming to the truth. But what we would need to do in this case is to grant safe conduct and ask the Dutch authorities to grant safe conduct as well. May I ask for your opinion on these issues, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we believe they are relevant. They have relevant information. I'm not going to make any comments about their credibility. We'll wait until we hear them. But as far as whether they are subpoenaed by the Defence or the Court, I think the Court can issue a subpoena on behalf of the Defence that the witnesses are required and are compelled to come here, just as you can on behalf of the Prosecution. But we have no preference. Whichever way the Court and the Defence want to handle it, whether they appear as Defence witnesses or Prosecution witnesses, and we have no objection to the safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll decide on this as soon as possible. Any other issues in addition to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it's for me to inform you that as you know, the Trial Chamber was seized by a motion of the OTP under Rule 66(C), and in balancing the interests mentioned in this Article 66(C) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Trial Chamber came to the conclusion to grant the request of the OTP. We are convinced that there will be no prejudice for Dr. Stakic or the Defence emanating from this decision. Then let us turn to next weeks' programme. We start, as we just said, with Witness 040. And here is no problem. We had the proffer already in the past. And additionally, the transcript, so therefore, this would enable the Prosecution immediately to start the cross-examination on Monday. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll be ready. Yes, Your Honour. We're not ready yet, but we will be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to mention the name, but we know the name of the witness of Tuesday. I think this will fill in the entire programme of Tuesday hopefully in a way that also follows the interests of the Prosecution and the Defence at the same time. But what about the remaining part of the week? Can we please hear the order of witnesses you want to call then and, as envisaged, that the proffers be provided on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The order in which we expect to call the witnesses, with the interruption of the witness that's coming on Tuesday, would be as follows: 040, 071, 072, and at the request of the Prosecution to be the last witness for the week would be 058. We do have a request in connection with this last witness, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I see my learned friend was on his feet. As the Court may know, 058, has testified in other cases before the Tribunal. We do not have access to his transcript of proceedings in the Keraterm case, Sikirica, and we would ask that the Court provide us, as well as to the OTP, or have the registry give us a copy of that transcript of that witness. And secondly, to inform the Court with respect to Witness 058, although initially we did not ask for protective measures, upon discussing the issues with him, we have been informed that since his last testimony, or better said, since the last time he testified here at The Hague before the Tribunal, he has experienced some problems in connection with that testimony. So now, we will be seeking protective measures for this witness. We can, if the Court would like, to prepare a written submission and would have that before the Court on Monday. We're just giving the OTP and the Court just a little advance notice in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this shouldn't be a problem. But may we hear the submission by the OTP, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objection to the protective measures. Just in regards to the order, because -- although we did ask for this week to hold off on Witness 58 because our search was not done, it is now complete. So actually, it's -- we're ahead on that than we are on 71 and 72. If there's no difference to the Defence, we would prefer that he precede those two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I hate to start following a practice, but if the OTP would prefer, if they want to set our schedule, that would work with us for the following week. It seems that it never works. When a witness that we call is deliberate in his mannerisms, the complaints are that he's too slow. The next day when we have a witness that seems to be rather quick in his responses, the complaint is that we are bringing witnesses that speak too fast. We will accommodate as we have in the past the OTP, and if it's their pleasure to call Witness 058 on Wednesday, we will do so. If we complete Witness 040 on Monday, we will immediately thereafter call Witness 058 on Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this cooperation. And I think we shouldn't try to find any kind of reason for dispute on this issue. I saw it just as a request, if possible, to hear 058 before 071. And if it's possible for you, I'm grateful. We would then proceed in this order for next week. Maybe for the record, because it was discussed only in the framework of the 65 ter meeting, what about the exhibits, please? First in B/C/S, and then step by step in a translated version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, to update the Court and the OTP, when we will introduce exhibits through witnesses, we will endeavour to provide those in B/C/S at least two days to the OTP so they could have their in-house people at least run a cursory review. But it's my understanding that they do have a complete set of our exhibits in the B/C/S version. We're still waiting for the translation department or unit to complete their translation of the documents that we submitted, and we do not have an anticipated time in which they would be complete with that translation or project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the Defence could do all of us a favour and present those documents immediately, and not wait until all the documents are translated, because also the capacities of this Trial Chamber are limited, and we really want to read what it is tendered by the Defence. And therefore, please, offer it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will do that with pleasure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then next point is related to the experts. During the 65 ter (i) meeting, and this is for the transcript, it -- we took the decision that with respect to the limited probative value, all the parties are no longer interested in having an expert on machine typewriting comparing the documents we have before us, whether or not they were written or printed by the same machine. So this issue is moot, and we will not expect any longer an expert on this. Finally, it's also for the transcript necessary to discuss the issue of the experts by the Defence. And may I, for the purpose of the transcript, hear what is the expected deadline from your point of view for having these expert statements ready in order to give the Prosecution the necessary and usual 40 days to decide whether or not to cross-examine the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did the Court say 40, 4-0, or 14, 1-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wasn't sure, because the transcript showed something else, and I did think I heard something. Before I give the Court a specific response to the timetable of the experts, I would like to at least respectfully continue to stand on the Defence's objection that we have not been provided with the necessary and adequate number of experts that we previously requested. I'm not asking at this time for the Court to revisit that; I just do not or would not like to engage in a conversation and not reiterate our objection on that. We strongly believe that the OTP has utilised numerous, in fact, several, at the very least, arguably more than two experts on issues before the Court in connection with this fourth amended indictment. We believe that our requests have been reasonable, consistent, and would be relevant on all those issues. And we understand, although respectfully do not agree, with the Court's decision to limit the Defence to two such experts. Nevertheless, in response to the Court's specific question, our expert, the academic historian, we believe will be prepared to submit his report to the Court and the OTP by February 15th, 2003. Our second expert, which is the military expert, will be prepared to submit his report on or about March 1st, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We discussed this issue this morning. And we came to the conclusion, taking into account the remaining days in March, that the absolute deadline for filing such an expert statement would be March 3. Having, then, 14 days for consideration by the Prosecution, there would be adequate time hopefully to call the witness. And I would kindly ask the Defence to make reservations in their calendar for both the historian and the military expert that they are prepared to appear as experts in this Trial Chamber before 21 March. I think it's necessary, experts normally don't have time at all. So therefore, if you could already now try to fix a date, it would be excellent because I think in all likelihood, the Prosecution intends to cross-examine the expert. 94 bis, what about 94 bis statements? When can they be provided? Sorry, 92 bis. Yes, 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will submit the proffers for the witnesses -- because the Court asked that question earlier and I failed to respond to it on Monday for the following group of witnesses in the detailed form that we believe we provided with the witness that appeared before the Court this afternoon. If the Court has any suggestions or requests to modify that, we would do so. With respect to the 92 bis statements, we hope to accomplish and conclude that within the next three weeks. Our one investigator is busy not only assisting transportation and other needs for the witnesses that are testifying here, he is overlapping in his duties and assisting in obtaining the final statements and getting them signed and executed by the proper authorities consistent with the Rules as outlined in 92 bis. So we believe, in essence, that within the next three weeks, we will be able to provide the Court with our complete set of 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any comments on this from the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No. We will need some time, of course, to review and see if we have objections, or we will ask for the right to cross-examine those witnesses once we see the statements. And I would suggest also that if the statements are complete in part, but not in whole, it's certainly helpful to us to get any of them so we can begin rather than waiting. There's no necessity from our point of view to wait until every witness's 92 bis statement is complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you live with this proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As soon as we receive them, Your Honour, we'll be happy to provide them to the Court and to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We also discussed this issue this morning. And we thought it appropriate that as we did it in the case of the Prosecutor's case, that we kindly ask the Defence to prepare, of course as soon as possible and produce as soon as possible, these statements, but no later than March 3. And the same is true for any kind of requests of amendments for additional witnesses or experts. Here also, the Trial Chamber imposes a deadline ending March 3. Until then, we expect motions, be it orally, be it in writing. But as you know, we prefer oral requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Again to reiterate, if we can get them in part, because if the Defence waited until the 3rd of March to give us 20 requests for 92 bis and we wanted to cross-examine all 20 of them, then we are running into big time problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, because as it reads everywhere, immediately but no later than the 3rd of March, only that we have already now clear lines and a clear deadline that the Defence knows after this 3rd of March, there will be no new requests accepted as regards new experts or new witnesses. And maybe for unforeseen reasons, there may be a delay related to the one or other 92 bis statement. But the deadline is March 3. Hopefully, we get it, of course, earlier. And as the cooperation between the parties was in the past good, I don't know why this should change in future. Anything else on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do have one other matter that we raised in the 65 ter conference, that it's my recollection the Court invited us to raise it with the full panel of Judges. But this may require us to go into private session at the request of the OTP, although we would prefer it to be in public session, because it involves one of the witnesses that the Court has ordered to appear sometime in the future, after sentencing. So I'm not sure how to proceed. Do you want me to continue with my request in open session, public session, or -- I need to be cautious because it was a request made by the OTP, that when we discuss this individual it goes into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we should try to make no secret of this issue. If possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understand we're talking about Mrs. Plavsic, but I believe what I indicated is that some items were provided to the Defence which are still provided on a confidential basis, and if we're discussing the contents of any of those items, at least at this point, it's confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you want to go into details of the contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just to reiterate my prior request in connection with the other interviews that were given by Mrs. Plavsic, we would like to reiterate that request. We haven't received those interviews yet. And I know that they are in existence. They have been distributed obviously to various members and team members of the OTP as well as Mrs. Plavsic's Defence team, which included approximately 6 or so people. We think that it's just a matter of spending 15 minutes and photocopying those pages. We haven't received those two interviews. We would like also to reiterate our request, although Ms. Ruth Karper said that we were going to get the B/C/S version hopefully by Monday for Dr. Stakic, we would just like to hold it to that date, give or take a day or two. We know that they are under some pressure as well, but we would like to keep it on a short leash. There is another request that I make in connection with Ms. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just step by step. I think there should be no problem to provide you with the requested documents. And I think it's -- there's some priority that Dr. Stakic is able to follow this tape in B/C/S. And I would kindly ask you if possible to provide Dr. Stakic on Monday with this tape. And please let us know whether or not Dr. Stakic has the necessary facilities to listen to this tape. And I take it we discussed it already in open court that Dr. Stakic will respect the in part confidentiality of this and not to discuss this with other inmates of the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the Defence can wait a few moments after court, it can be provided today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not a audiotape, it's actually a videotape it's my understanding that will be provided to Dr. Stakic. And he does have the capacity to view the videotape, and if not, we will advise the Court and perhaps with your assistance it can be accommodated or one can be provided to him for that limited purpose to review the videotape of the interviews. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you on this point, but I did have two other points in connection with Mrs. Plavsic. And again, I'm not sure if I should raise it. It doesn't come directly from the interview, but it includes two specific aspects that we requested at the 65 ter conference. One involves the wiretaps and the intercepts of conversations with Biljana Plavsic that she had that are in the possession of the OTP. And the second issue arrives from the Rules of the Tribunal, which is specifically Rule 68 involving Biljana Plavsic. We believe, since Biljana Plavsic is identified as a co-conspirator on each and every one of the counts in the fourth amended indictment against Dr. Stakic, it's not only relevant but it's reasonable that all those documents should be produced given the fact that she is testifying, but in my opinion, should have been produced even during the outset of Dr. Stakic's case. If the allegation is that there was a joint criminal enterprise, as there is, and maintaining that position not to provide the Defence with the 68 -- Rule 68 materials for any or all of the purported co-conspirators of this "joint criminal enterprise," I think prejudices the Defence, and I think we should have been provided that material well in advance of her testimony. Nevertheless, as it has been the practice in an attempt to cure any prejudice, we would be willing to accept for this one time the fact that they can produce to us the Rule 68 disclosures of Biljana Plavsic. But we would like that as soon as possible, since we know it's readily available and in their possession, as well as the wire intercepts. And obviously, we will continue to maintain the confidentiality requests as imposed on us by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I recall from the 65 ter, we discussed this, and my recollection was Your Honour ask the Defence for a written motion. We don't normally request that but in this particular case, especially since really this requires a lot of coordination with another team in the Prosecution that we don't have daily contact with, that would be very helpful to us to get it in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, we discussed this that way because there were also in other cases similar motions. And to treat all Defence teams in an equal way, may I kindly ask you a very short motion on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll provide the Court with the motion. We just can't promise that it will be very short, because it is a very important issue. But we hope to provide that by mid-week next week, and we will work during the breaks to complete it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This was the first related issue. And the second?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the two within that one issue, were the wiretaps and Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the related issue to that is if we review the indictment, there are other co-conspirators. There are other defendants that appear. There are other Rule 68 materials that have been provided to other Defence teams before this Tribunal. If there's an insistance on this joint criminal enterprise, we think that that will ultimately be the next step that the OTP would have to share with us. I also would like just for the record because I'm compelled not to allow the comment by the OTP a little earlier, and now I'm transgressing a little bit, with respect to credibility of witnesses. I dare say the Court has not invited us to comment on the credibility of witnesses. If the OTP felt that the six witnesses that they took the statements and interviews from were not credible, they should set forth exactly in writing why they think they are or are not credible. Quite frankly, to sit here in advance, in advance of the Court calling these witnesses, to pass judgement on individuals, when in fact if a cursory review of both Ms. Sutherland's and Mr. Koumjian's interrogation of these witnesses I don't believe that any person with any type of legal education, much less a judge, would find that those interviews were conducted in a fair manner, that those were interviews were conducted with all the documents before the witness. So I take exception to that comment, and that was the point that I would like to raise and think that this Court should make a decision on their credibility and not Mr. Koumjian. And I invite the Court to rule on the questions that were asked of these witnesses; not only were they misleading and speculative, but there were complete errors in connection with the questions asked of those witnesses. And then to have him suggest that they have a lack of credibility -- thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure if you're waving at me or asking me to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think enough is enough. And I don't want to re-emphasise. This is not a jury. Here are sitting three professional Judges, and we know to read, and we know what is our duty. And we can't leave it to one or the other party to decide on the credibility of the one or other witness. To that extent, the Trial Chamber, in fact, has the last word, if not later, the Appeal Chamber. But to be serious, I don't think we should go into details and stating that the one or other statement was taken in an inappropriate way. And we shouldn't go into premature allegations of nondisclosure of 68 material. I don't think in the moment, we don't have any indicia for this. The Prosecution is aware of their ongoing -- of the ongoing duty to comply with Rule 68, and I have no doubt at all that this will be done. Any other issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then from the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then may I take the opportunity at the end of this week, what is normally -- forms normally part of a Status Conference, but this would be due now. And normally we do it in the framework of a public hearing. May I ask you, Dr. Stakic, do you have any health problems in the moment, health problems more than all the participants in this Tribunal in the moment have, or do you have any complaints about the condition in the United Nations Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am satisfied with your wish for these proceedings to be over as quickly as possible. However, the introduction of work in two shifts, meaning the whole day work, I find it very exhausting because I have to spend here in this courtroom long hours, between 8.00 in the morning, until 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon. There's no way for me to get a walk outside. All I get to eat is a sandwich. But even more important than that is I have been deprived of the opportunity to meet with my counsels. And therefore, they have been also restricted in their opportunity to meet with the witnesses. I don't want to object to the schedule that has been adopted for next week, but I would kindly ask you to make sure that this does not become a practice because my digestive system is weak, and it's going to be very difficult for me to adapt to that, to spend so much time in closed confinement with no daylight and poor alimentation. Thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to address the Honourable Court. And I heard that you will consider this issue that I have just raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stakic. This concludes today's session. And I want to be on the safe side. We are starting on Monday at 9.00 or at 9.30?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: On Monday we sit from 9.00 to 12.00, and from 1.30 to 4.30 in courtroom II, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. We'll stick to the schedule the next week. The week after that is a usual week, as we proceeded in the past. And we have to, in fact, reconsider the schedule of the then following week. Thank you. I wish a good weekend to everybody, and first of all, good health. The trial stays adjourned until Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
